0.body: These pages describe the design and the technical architecture of The Seeker. The same Markdown files render on GitHub and build into the documentation site . API documentation for the Rust crates is published at theseekergame.github.io/api . Section Read it for Game Design The vision: audience, art direction, lore, the open brand, and intended mechanics Architecture How the game works: actor behavior, the timing and audio model, and level generation Authoring How to add content: asset guidelines and the script and animation formats The source code and authored assets define current behavior. Design pages record intent, and architecture pages explain the contracts the implementation preserves. When a page and the code disagree, trust the code and fix the page. Project-wide guides live in the repository root: README.md : what the game is and how to build and run it. CONTRIBUTING.md : how to set up, verify, and submit changes. AGENTS.md : the source map and the runtime rules every change must preserve. It is written for AI coding agents and is equally useful to people.

101.body: Field Default Meaning time_base "Relative" Origin for nonperiodic tick/time actions: playback initialization time_base = "Level" — Origin from LevelLoadTime, when supplied by the game time_base = "Startup" — Origin at simulation time/tick zero tick_quant Unset Quantizes the selected start tick , independently of the time origin and animation cadence Entity TimeBase and ScriptTickQuant components override the corresponding asset settings. All time origins use game simulation time, which pauses with the transport, rather than wall time. Quant strings have the form "N", "N+offset", or "N-offset", with positive N. A pattern matches when (value - offset) % N == 0. For start-tick quantization the implementation uses value - (value - offset) % N; for example, start tick 13 with tick_quant = "8+4" selects origin 12. It does not defer the entire script until a future tick: start actions and animation initialization still run when playback starts. Keep offsets within the intended origin range; the parser does not comprehensively validate unsafe quant values such as zero periods. tick_quant does not adjust the seconds origin and does not control run_every_n_ticks. Leave it unset unless that distinction is intentional. Use animation frame_clock for global/local frame cadence.

102.body: Field Example value Runtime behavior run_on_playback_control "Start" or "Stop" Initialization or normal playback shutdown/changeover run_on_slot_enable "Attack" A slot changes from false to true run_on_slot_disable "Attack" A slot changes from true to false run_at_tick 96 or [12, 16, 18] Nonperiodic offsets from the selected start tick run_every_n_ticks "64" or "12+8" Periodic matches against the absolute game tick run_at_millis 250 or [100, 200, 300] Nonperiodic offsets in milliseconds from the selected time origin run_at_time "1:13:17.315" or ["1:00", "2:00"] Nonperiodic duration offsets from the selected time origin Nonperiodic tick/time actions become eligible when elapsed tick/time is strictly greater than the requested value. Consequently run_at_tick = 0 executes on the following tick; use "Start" for initialization. Catch-up queues all overdue nonperiodic entries, retaining their original timestamps for audio scheduling. A periodic trigger checks only the current absolute tick and does not replay missed matches. For example, run_every_n_ticks = "16" matches global ticks 0, 16, 32, …; "12+8" matches 8, 20, 32, …. These phases do not restart when the script starts. run_at_time accepts quoted seconds, "minutes:seconds", or "hours:minutes:seconds", with optional fractional seconds; "5:80" is equivalent to "6:20". Setting an already-enabled slot to true does not trigger it again. Slots are local to the player/runtime. They can be changed by Rust or by the slot actions below.

11.body: The deepest layer of The Seeker is inspired by the idea that mathematics could be the foundation of reality, consciousness, and even emotion. A triangle can be defined as three connected points, but it can also be an experience, just as red feels different from green and one musical interval feels different from another. The aim is to let players experience mathematical relationships rather than only understand them: how primes feel compared with even numbers, or how a Fibonacci sequence feels compared with a fractal. Everything is tuned around one fundamental number, 12 : Standard animations run at 12 frames per second. Music is built on a 48 Hz reference, two octaves above the animation rate, using a tuning of pure mathematical ratios. The rhythm is 90 BPM, the same fundamental several octaves lower. Tiles are 6×6 pixels, and the player is 12 pixels tall. The result is meant to feel resonant and meditative. Players aren't told about it; at best it simply feels good. The player becomes an instrument too: steps, strikes, and impacts land on the shared musical grid. From that foundation, levels, music, and motion can explore different mathematical ideas, such as platforms sized in prime multiples or melodies built from a sequence, and combine them in unexpected ways.

110.body: Both accept current_script_only (default true) and optional label. StopAudio selects SFX; StopBackgroundAudio selects ambience. Neither stops the music bus. 111.body: Script requests commit in ScriptSet::Init and execute in ScriptSet::Run during GameTickUpdate. Action filters and slots can affect later actions in that update. Entries sharing a nonperiodic timestamp retain their authored order within that trigger list. Do not assume different trigger families form one globally timestamp-sorted script list; the mixer independently orders submitted audio commands by sample position and submission order. A common script finishes once its nonperiodic tick/time lists are exhausted and it has no periodic tick actions. Slot listeners and queued delays do not keep it alive. For a persistent listener, author an intentional periodic action or use a game-owned lifetime; merely declaring run_on_slot_enable is insufficient. An animation's extended tracker also contributes its playback lifetime. Normal stop and replacement run "Stop" actions. Despawning the entity directly removes the runtime without promising a final script update, so do not rely on a stop action as the sole cleanup mechanism for resources that must be released on arbitrary despawn. Playback completion itself does not despawn the entity. Global pause freezes simulation and scheduled gameplay audio together. Individually pausing a script stops its updates but does not freeze every voice it previously started. See the timing architecture for recovery and presentation behavior.

112.body: An .anim.toml asset describes sprite playback, frame cues, and optional script actions. It combines an image, atlas metadata, and a playback definition. The format reference lists the supported fields. Gameplay uses a 96 Hz simulation clock. An eight-tick frame has a 12 Hz cadence. The game defaults to global cadence: the first frame enters immediately and subsequent frames join the shared grid. These are simulation events; the renderer presents their historical poses with a small delay. See Timing, Audio, and Animation for the transport and presentation design.
112.title: Animations

113.body:
Place animations beneath assets/animations/. At startup, game/src/assets.rs recursively scans .anim.toml files and reads their [asset] metadata: [asset]
key = "anim.example.Pulse"
image = "animations/example/Pulse__r1c4__32x32.png" [settings]
ticks_per_frame = 8
frame_min = 1
frame_max = 4
frame_start = 1 This example assumes a matching image exists. Its path is relative to assets/. The filename declares one row, four columns, and 32×32-pixel cells. The scanner registers anim.example.Pulse, anim.example.Pulse.image, and anim.example.Pulse.atlas. Use keys = ["anim.example.Pulse", "anim.example.OtherPulse"] instead of key for aliases. New files or registration metadata require rerunning the startup scan. Frame numbers are one-based, traversing the sheet left to right, then top to bottom. Keep them within the atlas capacity. The image dimensions should match the declared rows, columns, and cell size. Shared images are allowed; do not combine sheets solely to satisfy a naming convention. Opaque magenta pixels (#FF00FF) in a frame mark its collider. engine/src/assets/sprite_colliders.rs covers the convex hull of each frame's magenta pixels with at most five rectangles and clears those pixels so they never show. Editing a mask or the sheet layout therefore changes combat geometry as well as the artwork.

119.body: The game recursively scans assets/animations/ for .anim.toml files. [asset] supplies one key or a list of keys, plus an image path relative to assets/. The image name must encode atlas dimensions, such as Strike__r1c8__32x32.png for one row, eight columns, and 32×32-pixel cells. Registration creates the animation key and its .image and .atlas keys. All authored frame indices are one-based ; Bevy's atlas index is zero-based. Frames traverse rows left to right, then top to bottom. Frame 1 is the first cell, and zero is invalid. The same atlas can serve several clips. Explicit image_asset_key and atlas_asset_key settings can select other registered assets. Keep frame ranges, bookmarks, cues, and seeks within the sheet's capacity. Do not depend on malformed input being rejected uniformly: some checks occur during game definition resolution, while generic playback assumes valid data.

120.body: Field Required/default Meaning ticks_per_frame Required, author a positive integer Frame period in 96 Hz simulation ticks frame_min Required Lowest frame in the default playback range frame_max Required Highest frame in the default playback range frame_start Required Initial frame when no clip section overrides it frame_clock Inherit application policy "Global" or "Local" play_reversed false Initially decrement rather than increment frame indices image_asset_key <animation-key>.image Registered image key atlas_asset_key <animation-key>.atlas Registered layout key time_base, tick_quant Common defaults Common-script origin settings , independent of frame cadence Without a clip override or script seek/loop, playback stops after the terminal frame's duration. It leaves the sprite at that frame; lifetime and visibility belong to the caller. The game's application policy is global; the generic engine default is local. Global playback enters the first frame immediately, then advances on strictly later global boundaries of the current period. With period 8 and start tick 5, frame entries occur at ticks 5, 8, 16, 24, …. The first frame is shortened. Periods 2, 4, 6, 8, and 16 all remain valid; a six-tick cadence is not forced into a power of two. Local playback counts each frame's duration from its own entry. An individually frozen global animation emits no catch-up entries and waits for the next strictly later boundary after thawing. Holding a frame does not repeat its entry actions. Display refresh and pixel rounding do not alter this simulation cadence.

[frame_bookmarks] maps names to absolute one-based frames. Each bookmark also emits a cue of the same name when its frame is entered. A numeric frame with frame_bookmark = "name" is relative to that bookmark: resolved frame = bookmark frame + numeric frame - 1 [frame_bookmarks]

action = "SetFrameNext"

flip_x = true The second action runs on absolute frame 13. Numeric target 2 relative to that bookmark would select frame 11. to_frame_bookmark overrides the entry's bookmark for SetFrameNow/SetFrameNext; an omitted target index defaults to 1, meaning the bookmark itself. A string-valued run_at_frame or current-frame condition resolves its named bookmark directly. Bookmark offsets never change run_at_tick or time triggers. Missing bookmarks fall back to frame 1 in generic script frame resolution; author valid names and use game definition validation rather than relying on that fallback.

126.body: All common-script parameters apply. Animation entries also accept: Field Meaning frame_bookmark Base for numeric current-frame conditions, frame triggers, and seek destinations if_frame_lt, if_frame_le, if_frame_gt, if_frame_ge Compare the authoritative current frame to a number or bookmark if_frame_is Equality condition; prefer a single number or bookmark (see limitation below) if_frame_is_not Exclude a number, bookmark, or any entry in a list if_oldanim_frame_lt, if_oldanim_frame_le, if_oldanim_frame_gt, if_oldanim_frame_ge Compare the preceding animation's frame at changeover if_oldanim_frame_was, if_oldanim_frame_was_not Match/exclude a literal frame or any literal frame in a list from that preceding animation if_playing_reversed true for reverse-only, false for forward-only; omission accepts either The current if_frame_is array implementation requires equality to every listed value. A list of distinct frames therefore never passes. Use a single value, bounds, or separate entries; do not treat it as an any-of test. run_at_frame arrays and if_frame_is_not arrays do use any-of matching. Old-animation frame conditions are absolute numeric indices from another asset; current bookmarks do not offset them. 14.body: The Seeker is an open-source brand: a shared sci-fi universe that anyone can play in, build on, and take in their own direction. The game in this repository, headed for a Steam release, is the trunk of the tree. The branches can be anything: other games, art projects, 3D worlds, music, prints, merch. The brand isn't owned by a company, or even by us. Its code, art, audio, and lore are open to everyone. Ownership is cultural, and it lives in our collectibles. Holders are the game masters of this shared world. Think of the Gamemakers in The Hunger Games , reshaping the arena while everyone else plays, minus the fight to the death. Holders help decide how the planet changes, which guardians watch over it, and where its story goes next. Anyone can play without owning anything; holders get to shape the world everyone plays in.

16.body: AI makes it possible to rebuild almost any product from a screenshot and a prompt. Copyright still exists, but when anyone can recreate a game in an afternoon, a creative project can't depend on it anymore. We saw this coming, and The Seeker has been open source from day one. So instead of fighting copies, we invite them. Open source spreads on its own: every fork, remix, and spin-off brings The Seeker's world to new people, and the best ideas can flow back into the original.
16.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Open Brand » Why open source
16.title: Why open source

17.body: Open source generates attention and culture, but on its own it gives the people who grow a brand no share in what it becomes. Collectibles fix that. Think of the first trading cards of a famous franchise: the bigger the world gets, the more they matter. Our collectibles work the same way for everything built on The Seeker. You help run the world. Holders are the game masters. They're planned to make real-time changes to the game world, place and customize characters on the planet, and steer how it evolves. Today they share a private chat with the team where suggestions shape the game, along with early releases and giveaways. The history is on-chain. We've been inscribing The Seeker's development on Bitcoin since 2023, starting with some of the first ten thousand Ordinals ever made. That timestamped record predates today's AI tools, and every version of The Seeker, whoever builds it, traces back to it. The game itself stays free of monetization. It's open source, playable without owning anything, and never pay-to-win. Collectibles capture the attention the brand earns instead of charging players for it. Design stays honest. Because the game isn't what's being sold, design decisions are made for the game, not for profit. There are no publishers or middlemen in between, and anyone can contribute as much or as little as they want. Collectibles are art and membership in the community. They aren't an investment product, and nothing here promises financial returns.

19.body: SEEKER NET brings the world to a new chain. It's a complete game and a social, economic, and art experiment of its own: 2,222 fully animated seekers charge toward activation, and the path each one takes becomes its final art. Every seeker below 9,000 charge gains 50 charge a day. At 9,000 it activates. Moving a seeker (a sale, a gift, or a transfer between wallets) releases a quarter of its charge, split evenly among every other seeker still charging. Every move makes everyone else stronger. Discharge is a seeker's latest release, and Uplink is everything it has ever given to the network. There are two quests. The main quest is charge: hold until activation. The side quest is Discharge and Uplink: power the network on the way there. No strategy is best, there are only different paths, and the rarest seekers will be the ones that took the paths fewer people chose. No new NFTs will be minted. Instead, top pixel artists keep adding traits to the existing seekers, until every decision, community participation included, shows up in the art.

24.body: The Seeker combines the exploration and movement of a metroidvania (think Hollow Knight) with the interlocking builds of an action RPG (Diablo, Risk of Rain) and the freedom of a sandbox. Underneath all three runs the idea at the heart of the lore : permutations . Every creature, material, skill, and choice should be able to combine with the others into something new, and the world should respond to how you play. Active Skills : weapons, the skill toolbar, and abilities copied from creatures Passive Skills : equipment that bends your stats and rules Platforming : how the Seeker moves Creatures and Ecosystem : the planet's life and how the planet fights back Each page separates what the game does today from where it is heading.

24.title: Gameplay and Mechanics

25.body: Descend. Explore procedurally generated caves that grow warmer, stranger, and more dangerous with depth, from icy upper caves into tundra below. Fight, copy, and gather. Copy the abilities of the creatures you meet, defeat them for Essence and drops, and harvest plants, berries, and ore from the caves. Return to a capsule. Capsules are your shelter. Store materials safely, spend Essence to research new recipes from what you carry, and craft devices, weapons, and passives. Build. Equip skills on the toolbar and passives in your inventory, and combine them into a playstyle. Push deeper , and the planet pushes back.
25.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » The core loop
25.title: The core loop

26.body: There is no quest log. The planet's pull draws the Seeker downward, and curiosity does the rest. Hidden rooms sit behind breakable walls, and familiar ground can change while you're away. The planet is hostile to Seekers. Their Alignment drains whenever they're away from a capsule or the tether network, and once it runs out they start taking damage that grows the longer they stay out. Tether nodes extend that safety outward, so the expedition literally grows from one shelter to the next, and portable tents give a place to rest out in the field. Death costs what's in your backpack. Everything stored in capsules, along with your skills, passives, weapons, and discovered recipes, carries over.
26.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Exploration
26.title: Exploration

27.body: Combat is fast and fluid. Attacking is meant to flow with movement rather than interrupt it, and skills are meant to synergize with very few incompatible combinations. The goal is countless distinct playstyles, so players explore the different ways of exploring the world as much as the world itself. Apart from a small starting kit and crafted devices, every ability is copied from a creature, complete with that creature's animation. Creatures also drop specific materials, so both the abilities and the recipes you want send you to particular parts of the planet, and what you find there opens up others. Fire and ice builds, stealth and backstabs, critical-hit chains, and deployed devices all pull a build in different directions.
27.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Combat and builds
27.title: Combat and builds

28.body: The long-term direction pushes the loop toward open-ended recursion: Become what you meet. Copying grows from single abilities toward fully becoming a creature for a while, with its movement and senses as well as its attacks. The planet adapts to you. Creatures evolve in response to your playstyle, and their new forms bring new abilities to copy. Materials remember. How you defeat something changes what it leaves behind, and with it what you can craft. The world changes. The caves themselves shift and harden as the planet reacts to the Seeker. These are directions rather than shipped features. The pages that follow describe where each one stands.

30.body: The Seeker carries melee and ranged weapons. The sword and hammer are melee weapons with their own reach, weight, and knockback; the hammer hits harder but slows you down. The bow fires arrows, which are a crafted resource. Weapon attacks have directional variants, so striking up, down, or forward while running, jumping, or falling all do what you'd expect.

32.body: Apart from the starting kit and crafted items, every ability is copied from a creature that uses it . To get a spinning attack, the Seeker learns it from a creature that spins; to get a dash, from one that dashes. A copied ability uses the creature's own mechanic and the creature's own animation : when you use it, you briefly take on that creature's form. The ability can be tuned for the player, with its own damage, timing, and reach, but its look and its origin stay recognizably the creature's. This ties the toolbar directly to the planet. Every creature you meet is a potential new ability, and building a playstyle means seeking out the creatures that have the abilities you want. Spit already works this way: the Seeker turns into a spider and spits venom at the nearest foe. Dash Strike copies the bat's dive mechanic to plunge through enemies and burst on landing, but still uses the Seeker's own animation. The current build still unlocks Dash, Whirl, Stealth, Dash Strike, and Flicker Strike through an experience-based Adaptation system. That system is being removed, and each of those abilities will come from a creature that uses it.

33.body: Flow over interruption. Attacks should blend with movement instead of rooting you in place, unless stopping is the point of the skill. Combine freely. Skills should synergize with each other, with passives, and with weapons, with as few incompatible combinations as possible. Every skill is a playstyle. Stealth rewards patience and backstabs, spinning and flickering attacks reward diving into crowds, and devices reward setting up the battlefield. Every ability has an owner. A new ability starts as a creature. Design the creature that uses it, then let the Seeker copy it.

33.title: Design principles

35.body: Passives are always on. Each one changes your stats or the rules of combat under some condition, and each one nudges you toward a particular way of playing. You can equip four at a time.

36.body: Crafted at capsules. Passives come from capsule recipes, so the materials you collect decide which ones you can make. Seven are craftable so far; the rest are implemented and still being worked into progression. Rolled values. Many passives roll a strength within a range when you get them. Upgrading improves the roll, and its description always shows the current value. Collected, then equipped. Unlocked passives wait in your inventory until you equip them, so you can swap builds back at a capsule. The passives implemented so far, grouped by the playstyle they encourage: Playstyle Examples Risk and low health Frenzied Attack, Serpent Ring, Vitality Overclock, Death Shroud Critical hits Flaming Heart, Obsidian Necklace, Critical Regeneration Position and movement Sharpshooter, Heavy Boots, Deadly Feather, Rabbit's Foot Stealth and backstabs Ice Dagger, Shadow Cloak Crowds and fresh targets Glowing Shard, Pack Killer, Prime Sygil Elemental conversion Fire Crystal or Ice Crystal (mutually exclusive) Extra effects Prism splits projectiles, Kinetic Orb adds orbiting orbs, Pulse Echo sends out melee pulses Skill rhythm Permutator rewards alternating skills; Pulse Drive turns Dash Strike crits into instant-skill triggers; Battery Pack adds a fifth skill slot Survival Bloodstone heals from experience orbs; Blood Shards turns overhealing into homing shards; Protective Spirit caps the damage of a single hit

37.body: Incentivize playstyles. A passive that rewards distance from enemies pushes you toward ranged builds and toward skills that slow or push enemies away. Each passive should suggest a way to play, not just a bigger number. Maximize compatibility. Passives should combine with each other and with active skills as freely as possible. Mutually exclusive pairs, like the two elemental crystals, are rare and deliberate. Combinatorial depth. Picking four from even a modest pool gives thousands of loadouts, before counting skills and weapons. The aim is that a large share of them feel genuinely different.

This game is meant to give you the sense of mystery and non-linear exploration known from Metriodvanias, combined with the deep character build customization and intense combat known from action RPGs, while also allowing the player to (for the most part) define their own path and goals while inhabiting a mostly 'natural' and un-scripted world, like in Sandbox Adventures.

40.body: Variable jump height. Release the jump button early for a short hop; hold it for a full jump. Coyote time. You can still jump for a moment after running off a ledge. Wall slides and wall jumps. Slide down walls and kick off them. Touching a wall restores your jump, so you can climb shafts by bouncing between walls. Dash. Bursts you past danger. Like every ability outside the starting kit, it's copied from a creature that uses it. Dash Strike dives straight down through enemies. Extra jumps. The Rabbit's Foot passive adds a double jump. Capsule lifts. Jump inside a capsule and drop through its hatch to ride the lift down. Spikes hurt and send you back to the last safe ground you stood on, so a mistake costs health and a little time rather than a long walk back.

41.body: Each world is assembled from validated chunk plans, so it's new every time while its routes stay traversable. Broad chambers give room for fights; shafts, ledges, and wall-supported climbs test movement between them. Secret rooms hide behind breakable walls, and the planet can grow new spikes into ground you've already crossed.
41.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Platforming » The caves as a course
41.title: The caves as a course

42.body: Platforming is optional depth. Difficult platforming should guard hidden areas and rewards, never the main journey. Being good at platforming should pay off without being required to enjoy the game. Movement and combat don't fight each other. You should be able to attack while running, jumping, and falling without losing control of the Seeker. Rhythm. Movement lives on the same musical clock as the rest of the game, so steps, jumps, and landings fall into the soundtrack's pulse.

42.title: Design principles

43.body: Optional platforming challenges are meant to become a bigger part of exploration, guarding hidden areas and rare materials. Learned creature forms should bring their own movement too: becoming a creature can mean moving the way it does.

43.title: Where it's heading

44.body: The planet's caves are full of life that grows stranger with depth. Creatures should feel like part of a living ecosystem rather than a list of enemies, and the planet itself should feel like it's paying attention to the Seeker.
44.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Creatures and Ecosystem » Creatures and Ecosystem
44.title: Creatures and Ecosystem

45.body: Creature How it behaves Spiders The most common ground hunters, small and large, in three tiers of strength, with darker tundra variants deeper down. Small spiders leap and bite; large ones keep their distance and shoot. Bats Four sizes, from small to huge, that patrol the air and dive at the Seeker. Buzzers Deep-tundra flyers that fire bursts of projectiles. Opi Deep-tundra ambushers that sit still until something comes close. Squid Hopping creatures of the deep caves. Void A dark pursuer that appears only when the planet is at its most hostile. Tentacles Trap creatures that strike from hiding (in development). Which creatures appear depends on depth and biome, and every population needs room to live: ground creatures need floor, flyers need open air. Defeated creatures leave materials behind, such as bat wings, and many recipes depend on them, so building toward a device or passive means hunting in the right part of the planet. Creatures are also where the Seeker's abilities come from. Apart from the starting kit and crafted devices, every ability is copied from a creature that uses it, and plays that creature's animation. A new player ability starts life as a new creature. See Active Skills . The caves aren't only hostile. Other travelers live down there too: the Vagrant and their yak, the Collector, the Monk, and the Exiled.
45.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Creatures and Ecosystem » Creatures today
45.title: Creatures today

46.body: The planet notices what the Seeker does. Its immunity rises as the Seeker kills and can ease off again, and the HUD shows its current level. As immunity climbs: creature populations grow larger; hidden spike patches start breaking out of the walls, changing ground you've already crossed; at its peak, the Void starts hunting the Seeker. Every fight changes the world a little. A careful, quiet Seeker meets a different planet from a reckless one.
46.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Creatures and Ecosystem » The planet's immune response
46.title: The planet's immune response

47.body: The original design organizes life around ecological roles, giving behavior a reason beyond attacking the player: Herbivores gather at oases where geothermal heat and water let plants grow, eat quickly, and retreat. They fight only to defend themselves, unless they're protecting their young. Carnivores patrol widely and wait near the oases for prey. They spot the Seeker from far away and give chase, and their young hunt alongside them. Scavengers search for leftovers. Alone they flee; in groups, or with young to protect, they grow bold. Beyond that core sit creatures like bats that attack anything nearby, and trap creatures that wait motionless until something comes close. The bigger direction is adaptation . Creatures should evolve in response to how the Seeker plays. Lean on fire, and the planet may answer with thicker hides, or with creatures that spit water to put it out. The Seeker can then copy those new abilities in turn, and how a creature is defeated changes what it leaves behind: a bat frozen solid or blown apart should drop something different from one cut down normally. The planet and the Seeker end up shaping each other, round after round.
47.breadcrumbs: Game Design » Gameplay and Mechanics » Creatures and Ecosystem » Ecology: where it's heading
47.title: Ecology: where it's heading

49.body: This is the design document for enemy and player state machines. The goal is readable, composable behavior with one execution algorithm per mechanic. Small Rust controllers decide what an actor does; reusable actions execute it; typed assets supply the variation. Adding an enemy that combines existing mechanics should require data. A genuinely new mechanic deserves a small, explicit Rust implementation.

50.body: Responsibility Owns Perception Target selection, visibility, reaction history, and physical observations Controller Decisions and the memory needed to make them Action Execution phases, commitment, cancellation, and temporary effects Motor Movement and collision response Presentation Sprite playback, procedural pose, orientation, and visual effects Enemy controllers use Combat, Wander, Hopper, or Ambush strategies. Patrol phases and decision timers belong to the controller. Grounded status and collision contacts are physical facts. Playing an animation does not reset decision timing. Engine code provides playback, collision, and the 96 Hz simulation clock. Game code owns controllers, action definitions, combat policy, and procedural enemy behavior. Keep transitions explicit and ordered; do not require every possible activation condition to be mutually exclusive.
50.breadcrumbs: Architecture » Actors and Actions » Separate decisions from execution
50.title: Separate decisions from execution

51.body: An action receives its owner, targeting information, damage attribution, motion parameters, and presentation binding. Its execution should not depend on whether input or AI selected it. Spider shots and player Spit share projectile execution. Bat dives and player downward dash share lunge execution. Their speed, direction, release timing, cancellation, damage, and artwork can differ through typed definitions. Copying an enemy ability means reusing the mechanic while allowing player-specific tuning. Apart from the starting kit and crafted deployable items, every player ability is copied from a creature: design the creature that uses it first, then bind the player's copy to the creature's mechanic and the creature's animation. Compose repeated behavior, such as Buzzer's projectile burst, through action parameters. Keep distinct algorithms explicit instead of building a general-purpose gameplay scripting language.
51.breadcrumbs: Architecture » Actors and Actions » Share mechanics across enemies and the player
51.title: Share mechanics across enemies and the player

52.body: Player locomotion owns idle, running, jumping, falling, and physical contact state. Skill admission owns equipment requirements, input buffering, cooldowns, stock, and sustained-use checks. Toolbar order resolves competing foreground requests; at most one succeeds per tick. Instant uses can succeed alongside it, regardless of their toolbar position. The foreground slot stores one typed execution. Mechanic-specific ECS tags only index that execution for queries; they do not store another copy of its state. Basic weapon attacks select their weapon and directional variant. Copied abilities bind shared mechanics to their own tuning and presentation. Existing dedicated mechanics use the same foreground lifecycle, so replacing their content does not require changing locomotion. Locomotion and the foreground skill are separate concerns. Locomotion keeps tracking the appropriate state and background presentation while an action owns selected outputs. Movement curves obey the foreground motion ownership and the player's hit-stop policies. Releasing an action lets presentation select the current locomotion animation without skill-specific restoration code. The player graphics record a resting anchor independently of an action's temporary offset. Releasing presentation restores that anchor only for the owned execution. Spike recovery suspends motion and action admission under its own lifetime, releases foreground resources, and resumes on a physically supported, hazard-free position after validating the destination again. The recovery anchor and combat's grounded classification have separate meanings. Passives modify stats and react to combat or skill events through their own systems. Independently living projectiles, deployed objects, and instant skills do not need to occupy the foreground action slot. Shared actions complement the player skill system; they do not require every skill to use the same execution algorithm. Instant placement/payment/effect execution is shared by input admission and Pulse Drive through skills/instant.rs, with an explicit activation origin for their different admission and stealth rules. Tent and tether hold/release previews share skills/placement_preview.rs; their placement evaluators and spawned-object simulations remain separate.
52.breadcrumbs: Architecture » Actors and Actions » Keep player control responsive
52.title: Keep player control responsive

53.body: An item can spawn immediately or use a foreground deployment action. Instant use spends available backpack stock and creates the object without taking movement or presentation ownership. A deployment can hold the player still, play a pinned once clip, and create the same kind of object at a named release cue. Deployment validates placement and reserves stock together when it starts. Reserved stock is unavailable to other uses or crafting. Placement is checked again at release. Cancellation before release refunds the reservation; release consumes it exactly once. Completing or interrupting the player action leaves an already deployed object alive under its own lifetime rules. Cooldowns and other activation rules remain at the skill layer; object behavior belongs to the spawned item.
53.breadcrumbs: Architecture » Actors and Actions » Treat items as independently living effects
53.title: Treat items as independently living effects

54.body: Each actor has one foreground action. The action declares which movement axes, facing, and presentation it controls. Resolve death, status effects, knockback, actions, and locomotion through explicit ownership and actor-specific precedence. Every execution has a unique identity. Completion, cancellation, interruption, and component removal release only that execution's temporary hitboxes and overrides. Cleanup is idempotent. Launched projectiles and other independent effects follow their own lifetimes. Dead or cancelled actions cannot emit stale combat effects.
54.breadcrumbs: Architecture » Actors and Actions » Make ownership and cleanup explicit
54.title: Make ownership and cleanup explicit

55.body: Decision clocks, action progress, and playback position remain separate. Sprite actions use authored frames, named cues, and once/loop/hold sections. Procedural actions use fixed-tick phases. Both obey the same action lifecycle and ownership contract. Playback emits ordered start, frame-entry/exit, cue, loop, seek, completion, and interruption events tagged with its execution ID. Consumers use the execution they own. A same-clip restart creates a new execution; holding a frame does not repeat its entry effects. Playback advances at most once per simulation tick, with requests committed at an explicit schedule boundary. Player admission commits before background locomotion and foreground execution; movement is resolved before collision-dependent combat effects. Deferred completion checks the execution identity at commit, so it cannot terminate a replacement action. Frame-authored walking is local displacement on actual frame entry. Locomotion explicitly selects continuous movement or frame steps. Each step passes through normal tile collision; blocked displacement is discarded. Actor movement uses pixels per tick, while projectile conventions remain explicit at their own boundary. Gameplay facing is world direction; native sprite orientation belongs to presentation. Procedural presentation does not need a fictitious sprite timeline. Tentacle geometry follows its authoritative fixed-tick pose, with attack timing and hitbox lifetime owned by the action. Void combines multipart presentation with the shared flying pursuit controller. Pursuit approaches a perceived target continuously and uses contact damage and its own contact cooldown, without entering a timeline attack activity.

60.body: Position Meaning Main types Device cursor Sample frames supplied continuously, including silence during pause AudioClock, callback snapshot Game transport Musical position mapped onto the device timeline; can pause or begin a new epoch GameTransport, MasterClock Simulation cursor Next tick to execute and the target admitted by the master clock GameTime, ClockTime Presentation cursor Musical moment selected for the expected display time RenderInterpolation, PresentationTime A transport epoch identifies one mapping between device frames and musical time. Resetting that mapping invalidates commands from the previous epoch. Ordinary tick advancement and lead adjustment keep the same epoch. GameTickPre → GameTickUpdate → GameTickPost executes every admitted simulation tick. Simulation runs ahead of playback so its commands can reach the mixer before their deadlines. The initial lead is four ticks (41.67 ms). Lead grows to cover sustained observed frame intervals, output latency, buffer duration, and a safety tick. It is rounded up to whole ticks and does not shrink during playback. Increasing lead only admits more future simulation ticks: it preserves the audio epoch, active voices, and every scheduled sample timestamp. A late-play diagnostic alone never resets the transport. The callback publishes coherent bounded snapshots: device position, host playback estimate, mapping, epoch, callback size, latency, and diagnostics. A full snapshot channel evicts an obsolete snapshot. Timestamp regression, implausible latency, and discontinuities fall back to callback arrival plus an estimated buffer of latency. Host-time estimation affects presentation and simulation admission, never scheduled sample positions. Frame-pacing calibration uses the 90th percentile of a complete 32-sample window. Intervals of 100 ms or more are loading/stall samples and do not enter this estimate. A few irregular startup frames cannot set the persistent lead before the window fills; longer sustained slow rendering can increase it without restarting playback.

61.body: Short rendering stalls execute the missing simulation ticks. A severe backlog starts an explicit epoch at the next unexecuted tick, silences stale voices, and restores soundtrack phase. It does not increment the gameplay tick past unexecuted work. The host estimate holds while awaiting the callback's epoch acknowledgment. Missing devices use monotonic silent time; device retries create a fresh epoch. SEEKER_SILENT_AUDIO=1 intentionally disables device access. PauseRequests combines manual P and modal menu, inventory, and capsule-panel ownership before frame clock admission, and derives GameState and GameTransport::paused together. Closing a modal preserves an independent manual pause; the menu's Resume action clears it. Simulation stops admitting ticks, and the mixer freezes music and SFX playheads at the scheduled boundary while continuing to supply silent device buffers. Resume preserves those playheads and replenishes scheduling lead. Menu/loading UI uses real time; gameplay presentation uses PresentationTime. Modal input flushes both gameplay action banks and buffered edges, so resume does not replay menu presses.

62.body: For a globally clocked eight-tick animation starting at tick 5, the first frame enters at tick 5 and the second at tick 8. If the second frame triggers an SFX, its onset is transport sample frame 4,000 at 48 kHz. GameTickPre → GameTickUpdate → GameTickPost executes tick 8. Script requests commit in ScriptSet::Init; playback advances in ScriptSet::Run and publishes ordered events. Cues, collision poses, and frame-driven movement use this authoritative entry. The script schedules the sound at tick 8. The engine converts that absolute timestamp into a sample position and flushes commands after each simulation tick. GameTickPost prepares actor and attachment transforms, then captures the tick-stamped sprite and camera poses. The audio callback applies the sound at sample frame 4,000, even if that position lies in the middle of its buffer. Rendering selects the historical pose for its estimated display time. The second sprite frame becomes eligible when that cursor reaches tick 8. The device epoch determines when sample frame 4,000 is heard in wall time. Scheduling lead gives simulation time to produce the event before then. It is not an extra delay added independently to each sound. When rendering catches up through several ticks, every simulation entry still executes even if the display cannot show every intermediate pose.

63.body: The output preference is 48 kHz stereo and 256 frames. Device negotiation can select another supported rate, channel count, sample format, or buffer size. Bevy AudioSource bytes are decoded and resampled on the async compute pool. SFX are prepared before the loading screen completes. Music is prepared on demand; only current, pending, and fading tracks remain decoded. Commands carry an absolute transport frame, epoch, and stable ordering number. Plays, stops, loops, voice gain ramps, and bus gains are applied inside callbacks at their offsets. Late one-shots advance into their remaining tails, or finish silently if their whole duration has passed. Their original onset is never shifted to a buffer boundary. SFX and background voices have separate fixed pools. SFX pressure steals the oldest SFX; it cannot steal music. Background exhaustion is reported, and the music controller can retry. Callback queues, scheduled storage, mixing scratch space, and voice slots are bounded. Decode, file access, logging, and heap allocation remain on other threads. Sample and completion pins outlive callback ownership, including stream shutdown, so the callback does not destroy their final heap allocations. Critical controls have a separate queue. Main-thread pressure or exhaustion of callback control storage requests explicit resynchronization instead of silently abandoning a stop or pause. Completion markers do not depend on an overflow-prone completion queue. AudioBus::Music, Ambience, and Sfx are independent. Actor scripts retain label/instance ownership. The yak's loop uses the Ambience label and cannot stop the soundtrack.

64.body: The engine default frame clock is local; the game installs AnimationClock(FrameClock::Global). Each asset can override it with [settings] frame_clock = "Local" or "Global". A global animation enters its first frame immediately. Later entries occur on strictly later multiples of its current frame period. An eight-tick animation starting at tick 5 enters its second frame at tick 8, then at 16, 24, and so on. Periods such as 2, 4, 6, and 16 remain valid. An individually frozen animation emits no catch-up entries on thaw; global playback waits for the next strictly later boundary. Holds, seeks, reversal, action ownership, and once-per-tick advancement remain authoritative simulation operations. Common-script tick_quant retains its script-origin meaning. Local cadence counts ticks from that playback's own frame entries. Global cadence aligns subsequent entries to the shared grid and can shorten the initial frame. Selecting a cadence does not change execution ownership. Common-script origin quantization and animation-frame cadence remain separate settings. Simulation sprites are the collision contract. AnimationCollider continues to reference the authoritative entity. Frame cues, displacement, collider selection, and audio commands use that tick's frame entry. Render-only proxies never carry actor ownership or colliders.

66.body: Continuous transforms interpolate between bracketing samples. Sprite atlas frames and visibility step at their recorded boundary. PresentationJump(tick) suppresses interpolation across teleports and frame-step displacement. PresentationPolicy exposes independent pixel_aligned and stepped state overrides. Player graphics remain pixel aligned by default in all existing states. PresentationAnchor gives equipment the same fractional-to-integer anchor correction as its player without changing gameplay parenting. Interpolation is useful even for a pixel-aligned player: selecting the position between two simulation samples before rounding gives the display the nearest pixel at the requested time. Rounding still produces deliberate pixel steps. Floating positions can be selected by a state policy without changing simulation or audio timing. Disabling interpolation holds the earlier sample until the next boundary; it does not change the animation cadence. Camera position and shake use the same presentation cursor. Particle emitter descriptors remain game owned while delayed Hanabi instances consume PresentationTime; equipment and attached sprites use historical poses. PresentationAlignment is captured with each sprite pose and copied onto its proxy before game-owned pixel-view alignment. Damage sparks use UprightCameraPixels, retaining camera alignment through logical despawn without recovering markers from a dead source. Foliage shader animation and gameplay visual timers consume presentation time. Display refresh is independent of the musical grid: AutoVsync, pipelined rendering, and a requested maximum frame latency of two remain enabled. Two permits more CPU/GPU overlap; one remains a comparison option for lower display latency. The backend treats this setting as a hint, not a measured display delay.

Use the recorded frame_latency and FPS to compare before recalibrating AV offset. macOS media-key mode requires Fn+F8. F9: show/hide the panel. F10: cycle test clicks off, callback-generated reference impulses, and impulses submitted by normal game ticks. Music and ordinary SFX keep playing. F11: compare pixel-aligned and floating player positions. F12: compare interpolated and held movement. [ / ]: change AV offset by 1 ms. P: pause/resume the transport. F10–F12 and AV-offset controls require the panel to be visible. F8 works with it hidden; P follows the game pause controls. macOS media-key mode may require Fn with any function key. target/timing-diagnostics.log is recreated at startup and records one row per second, plus pause/resynchronization changes. It includes device health, late plays/controls, callback gaps/cost, history usage, music selection/volume, and presentation settings. SEEKER_TIMING_LOG overrides its path. Logging stops after 86,400 rows to bound disk usage. File writes run on the main thread, never in the audio callback. Rows also aggregate FPS, mean/worst frame intervals, main-world work, and simulation work across the entire interval; frame_ms alone is only the latest frame. Main-world measurements run from First to Last and exclude render-subapp work and subsequent frame-pacing waits. The probe text refreshes on 12 Hz frame changes rather than every display update. Render-thread aggregates separate preparation (including acquiring the next surface texture) from submission/presentation/cleanup. These wall times include driver waits; they do not measure GPU execution time. Render and main-world work overlap and must not be summed as CPU utilization. Rows include window physical resolution and the number of focused frames; Bevy throttles unfocused windows, so compare focused intervals in the same scene and exclude loading hitches. The panel alternates at 12 Hz and shows tick/frame/beat/bar numbers. It reports output settings, scheduling lead, estimated output latency, late plays versus controls, maximum lateness, queue pressure, stolen voices, callback cost, callback gaps, timestamp fallbacks, history use, and resynchronizations. Callback gaps are a portable underrun symptom, not proof that a particular backend dropped samples. SEEKER_DISPLAY_LATENCY_MS defaults to 16.667 and estimates extraction-to-display latency. SEEKER_AV_OFFSET_MS defaults to zero; a positive offset selects a later visual moment to compensate for a slower display. Neither setting changes audio sample timestamps. Calibration cannot identify speaker, Bluetooth, display processing, or scanout delay from software timestamps alone. Offline tests establish sample placement, rational conversion, pause phase, ordering, cancellation, crossfades, exhaustion, recovery, animation cadence, history lifetime, and presentation sampling at 59.94/60/75/120/144 Hz and variable intervals. Hardware observation is still needed for physical AV alignment. A 12 Hz frame can span different numbers of refreshes, especially at 59.94 Hz: eight clicks per logical animation frame does not imply eight clicks in every physical screen hold.

69.body: Use GameTime and fixed-tick schedules for gameplay. Use PresentationTime for gameplay visual time, and Time<Real> for menu/loading UI. Rendering may read history but must not emit gameplay cues or decide damage from the displayed sprite. Add rhythm constants and conversions to the shared grid. Schedule sounds through AudioEngine or the existing script actions; do not add another output stream or a render-frame timer for rhythmic events. Keep stop labels scoped to their bus and execution. Mark sprite teleports and frame-step movement with PresentationJump; do not assume a component used by one presentation path automatically applies to every other path. A displayed effect may outlive its logical source, but cannot keep that source's gameplay ownership alive. Keep callback work bounded and retain shared buffers until their last callback reference has been released. Prefer removing measured redundant work over changing cadence, reducing simulation frequency, or sacrificing event ordering. Sprite proxies update render layers directly and avoid unchanged transform/visibility writes. The shared PixelView derives the presented camera position, physical viewport, integer gameplay scale, raster center, and rounded residual once per render frame. 7.body: Seekers are explorers in the service of Theorem , a vast organization devoted to discovering and formalizing knowledge across the universe. Seeker is a role, not a species: humans, aliens, and machines alike can become one. The seekers of SEEKER NET , for example, are tiny, computer-like robots. What Seekers chase are permutations of existence . Seeing ultraviolet light is one kind of existence. Thinking as a swarm is another, and so is living beneath an ocean of ice. Combine them and you get something no being has felt before: a swarm-mind drifting under the ice, perceiving colors no eye has ever seen. Seekers crave these combinations. They have already found the familiar ingredients, so they travel ever farther in search of strange ones, the kind that make every earlier combination feel small. A few ideas shape the life of a Seeker: The Codex is Theorem's shared archive of everything its Seekers have recorded. A Seeker reaches it through their visor to scan, record, and analyze what they find. Attunement is the ability to sense the frequencies and structures of other beings and of the cosmos itself. Seekers learn it through training, collaboration, and meditation before setting out alone. Solitude. Seekers travel and work alone, far from the organization that sent them.

71.body: The goal is a varied, readable cave world with rich pixel artwork and inexpensive gameplay rendering. PNG plans define traversable geometry and authored markers. Shared generation rules supply rock mosaics, vegetation, objects, and biome detail. Prepared surfaces and local state changes let the planet become harsher as the player explores without generating textures during play. Keep logical world data separate from its presentation. Reuse a small number of algorithms, preserve authored constraints, and measure complete workloads. Favor removing repeated work over adding caches, scheduling frameworks, or special cases. This is the single design and authoring document for the level-generation system; source code and assets establish exact tuning.

72.body: Responsibility Owns Request Seed, selected map, generation configuration, and build identity Asset catalog Loaded artwork, decoded masks, parsed rules, and filename metadata Assembly Compatible chunk selection, flips, palette compilation, and authored markers Geometry Secret-room carving, terrain/hazard state, and collision inputs Cosmetic generation Mosaic categories, depth biomes with geyser patches, and decoration/object placement Surface baking Native artwork, edge darkening, backgrounds, concealment covers, and prepared alternatives Darkness CPU coverage, sky visibility through every parallax layer, and a distance-field bake into R8 light Publication Collision, enemy placement catalog, render assets, and readiness Adaptation Persistent world-change state and activation of prepared products The dependency order is load assets → assemble map → carve rooms → generate terrain mosaics → place geysers and determine biomes → place decorations and objects → prepare surfaces and adaptations → publish collision, enemy catalog, and darkness → ready . Near-background generation consumes the carved terrain and biome data. Middle/far backgrounds are built offline and loaded as a selected pair. GenerationRequest chooses a random seed for normal games and accepts a fixed seed for diagnostics. A seed reproduces a request with the same assets and algorithms; it is not a promise of identical output across code or content changes. GenerationBuild owns an identifier and explicit Assets, Ground, Background, Surfaces, Publishing, Ready, or Failed phase. No timeout skips missing darkness dependencies. Readiness requires collision and enemy data, completed darkness, required image uploads, and a render pass with no waiting pipelines. Restart discards world products and rejects publication from an old generation.

73.body: Map PNGs live under assets/levels/maps. A map pixel represents one 96×96-tile chunk: black is an ordinary occupied cell, white selects the unique player-spawn template, and #45ff00 requests geyser content. Transparent cells are empty. Arbitrary rectangular images are cropped to occupied bounds; holes remain holes. Chunk PNGs live under assets/levels/chunks. Their final underscore suffix declares connectors in U, D, L, and R directions, such as generated_chunk_0042_UDR.png. The runtime indexes connector-compatible templates and their horizontal flips. It exhausts compatible unused templates before deterministic reuse. The spawn template remains unique. Selected pixels compile directly into world arrays without a composite-PNG round trip. large_chunk_3x3_<number>_<connectors>.png plans are 288×288 tiles. Assembly reserves a complete occupied 3×3 block before assigning ordinary chunks, provided every external neighbor meets the middle cell of an edge and the block contains no spawn cell. A large plan exposes centered twelve-tile ports on those middle edges and seals its corners. Each matching large plan is consumed once per world; exhausted pools fall back to ordinary chunks. Logical slices preserve the plan's continuity, while collision, decoration quotas, adaptations, and rendering keep their existing 96×96 regions. tools/generate_demo_map.py authors the demo map with 64 connected cells, sixteen depth rows, loops, and three eligible large-room blocks. Generated terrain starts in ice, blends in coarse patches from four to six chunks below the spawn row, and uses tundra below that. Geysers add local tundra patches. The baseline biome also controls decoration and object eligibility; it is not limited to terrain colors. A custom level PNG uses the same tile palette and bypasses chunk selection. PNG rows point down; world Y points up. Tiles are six world pixels by default and terrain artwork is six pixels per tile. Palette classification ignores pixels with alpha below 128. Paint exact colors without anti-aliasing. Tile-plan color Meaning #000000 Solid terrain #FFFFFF Active spikes #808080 Optional spikes, initially solid terrain #FFFF00 Player spawn #BB5E02 Vagrant/yak pair #456368 Collector #FFEEC3 Monk #654170 Exiled #928C8C Capsule marker #4DFBFF Ore marker #5B666F Manual near-background coverage The compiler resolves capsule placement in the player-spawn chunk. Enemy populations come from collision-driven habitat analysis; they are not inferred from arbitrary blue pixels. Spike recovery points are runtime physical anchors rather than authored PNG markers. Content placement excludes empty map cells and the exterior air above the first rock in an occupied chunk with no chunk above it, except for the playable spawn crater. This filter runs before rule quotas and spacing, so inaccessible outer tops do not consume content budgets. Enemy habitat analysis uses the same filter. Generation PNG filenames carry numeric rule ordering, probability, permitted pattern flips, random output flips, sprite weights, offsets, spacing, and placement limits. catalog.rs is the parser for those conventions. Preserve rule order and distinguish a pattern flip used for matching from an artwork flip used for variety. Rule-mask images are authoring data, not terrain texture layers.

74.body: Carve all startup rooms before running terrain mosaic rules. These rules depend on terrain edges: a room's inner wall and an isolated platform inside it need the same category generation as an outside platform. Clipping categories generated for an unbroken wall cannot create the missing transitions around a new cavity. Generate the three mosaic masks once for the carved terrain. Each layer consumes the preceding layer's output, and higher layers own overlapping cells. Secret-room covers and optional-spike alternatives reuse this cosmetic structure, clipped to their terrain state. Runtime activation does not rerun mosaic rules. LDtk selects the actual tiles from a complete category grid. Terrain values are Wall0/base 18, mosaic1 17, mosaic2 19, and mosaic3 20; spikes have their own category. An empty mosaic result uses distance-based categories as a fallback. The category grid and the pixel-distance shading field have different purposes and must not be substituted for one another. Terrain rule priority is spikes → wall0–wall3 → fog1–fog3 → fog_add. The first priority stage producing a tile wins. Within a stage, authored ordering, probability, allowed flips, and break_on_match control the result. Unresolved cells use catchall tiles discovered from the LDtk data. Tundra grass is evaluated only where the tundra terrain program leaves a cell unresolved. Biome selection happens before per-cell rule evaluation, while matching can still read neighboring values from the full grid. LDtk pattern 0 ignores a neighbor, positive N requires that value, negative -N forbids it, 1000001 requires any occupied value, and -1000001 requires empty. Out-of-world LDtk samples are empty. Near-background rules evaluate fog transitions before wall catchalls and see all category boundaries in their plane. Background values 1, 2, and 3 describe main/middle/far wall categories; tundra also uses near-wall 4. These categories are not additional parallax planes.

75.body: Secret-room PNG rules live under assets/levels/secret_rooms. Offsets are relative to the image center; a _ruleflip-x filename allows horizontal matching. Each rule is placed at most once, with deterministic scoring among valid anchors. Room-rule color Meaning Black Carve room air White Carve the breakable entrance and create its cover #5B666F Carve and add manual near background #4DFBFF Carve and add an ore marker #6ABE30 Require rock without carving it #AC3232 Require existing cave air without spikes Entrances are checked against the original assembled cave, so the air created by one room cannot serve as another room's entrance. Carved cells and breakable entrances must be terrain. Placement-only requirements do not become cover pixels or collision tiles. A rule with no valid placement is skipped. The playable geometry, mosaic detail, and exposed-wall shading are prepared at startup. A room's cover is the level as it was before carving, over the room and the border its carving reshades (cover_border_tiles: the reach of edge shading plus a tile). Covers never show: every room stays two borders away from other rooms, optional spikes, and the tiles the intro impact changes. So no carving reaches another room's cover, no cover hides art that changes during play, and each cover matches the ground wherever it ends, whichever rooms are open. Covers are baked with the level's decorations; decorations anchored in a room are drawn on a hidden contents sprite instead of the ground, since they could reach past the thin wall into the entrance. For the same reason, entity placement skips room tiles; rooms hold only their authored ore. Temporary collision contributions keep a room closed until its entrance breaks. The breakable wall takes five hits; opening removes its wall entity, room cover, and dynamic collision contribution, and reveals the room's contents. Room opening performs bounded entity/collision changes, with no image baking.

76.body: Optional spikes express the planet's increasing hostility and make backtracking surprising. PreparedAdaptation owns stable identity, available states, affected chunks, prepared visual handles, terrain/hazard deltas, and entity activation data. Logical adaptation state is separate from disposable rendering assets. Startup prepares the initial terrain once and alternative images only for affected regions and their required margins. Nearby spike markers that influence the same surfaces share an activation group. Activation remains one-way, starts at immunity 2, evaluates every 16 game ticks, and waits until the group is outside the player's two-chunk active radius. Disabled hazard entities are prepared with their images. Activation switches prepared material handles, updates tile state, patches base collision while retaining secret-cover contributions, and enables the hazards before simulation observes the new state. Repeated activation is harmless. No normal activation performs rule matching, texture baking, or a whole-world collision rebuild. Use this interface for additional adaptations when their behavior fits. An adaptation changing background openings or light coverage needs explicit prepared background/darkness outputs and a publication contract; a generic darkness-patch consumer is not implemented. 77.body: Render output uses 96×96-tile regions at native artwork resolution. Each region reads enough neighboring input for tile edges, shading, decorations, and blur. Global coordinates control dithering and sampling; internal output borders are not world edges. Up to four Bevy task-pool workers bake independent regions with reusable scratch storage. Ordered logical decisions remain deterministic. Ground darkening uses Euclidean distance from exposed terrain edges, the established falloff, linear-color attenuation tables, and global-coordinate dithering. Transparent pixels are skipped. The distance implementation is shared with darkness. A ground bake reads an 11-tile input margin for the current shading support. Decorations are indexed to contributing output regions and composited with their existing alpha and placement rules. The near background, described below, is warped for its parallax depth. Depth biomes receive bounded geyser-radius stamping with the existing inner/outer rings and authored chunk restrictions. Spacing indexes and sparse decoration ownership keep placement checks local. Gaussian background blur uses linear premultiplied color, horizontal/vertical passes, and one conversion in each direction. Texture gutters and kernel margins preserve continuity. Terrain uses nearest sampling; blurred background textures use their existing filtering. All regional pieces of a parallax plane share a common world center and transform. The farthest cave plane represents distant light. Openings in nearer cave walls allow that light through; depth and the player's backlight supply the rest of the feel. A baked foreground-darkness layer and inexpensive fullscreen composition express this without dynamic lights or shadow maps. Darkness consumes compact CPU coverage from unblurred terrain/background artwork, including relevant decoration alpha. The lightmap has two pixels per tile. A pixel is a light source where a camera centred on it would see through the ground and every background layer to the sky; parallax shows a layer at depth d with its content d times nearer the layer's centre. One distance field over the lightmap gives every pixel the light of its nearest source: full at the source, fading with the square of the distance to nothing at 24 world units. Chunks outside the map hold no sources. The bake depends on neither the camera nor the window, and the loading screen waits for it. The result is stored in bounded 2,048-pixel texture-array pages with gutters and an R32Uint page table. No redundant RGBA mask textures or source cameras are needed. The fullscreen pass darkens by depth below the surface, then baked light and the player's backlight each lift a share of that darkness, and dithering hides 8-bit banding. DarknessSettings in darkness.rs documents the uniform the pass reads.

78.body: The artist's hand-made LDtk level defines the look of every background plane. tools/backgrounds/exemplars.py extracts its middle, far, and near IntGrid layers for both biomes into exemplar PNGs: tools/backgrounds/source/exemplars/ for the offline planes and assets/levels/tiles/<biome>/near_bg/exemplar.png for the near plane. Each color is one IntGrid value, black marks the artist's terrain, and transparent cells lie outside the painted area. The artist's project is not part of this repository, but the extracted exemplars are; rerun the extraction only when that reference changes. The same LDtk rules turn these values into tiles, so reproducing the artist's values reproduces the artist's tiles. Generation separates where a plane opens from how its wall is detailed : Openings. The near plane follows the carved terrain (background_openings.rs): it hugs most terrain surfaces with a skin up to five tiles thick and leaves the rest bare, swells into occasional masses up to about eleven tiles beside the terrain, bridges gaps up to about six tiles wide, and leaves the cave farther from terrain open. Middle and far planes cannot see the terrain: openings.py places the artist's own openings, flipped for variety, in wavy horizontal strata as the artist does. Far openings gather behind middle openings so light reaches through. Strata are laid out in view space and sampled through each plane's parallax depth, so the planes line up wherever the camera stands. Spacing. Walls between neighbouring middle/far openings are at least three tiles thick, openings keep three tiles from the covered area's edge, and every opening is one whole artist opening. Near openings are never one tile wide, near wall never floats or thins to a strand in the air, and near openings smaller than 40 tiles close. Detailing. Image analogies (synthesis.py offline and background_synthesis.rs at runtime) copy each wall cell's value from the exemplar cell whose surrounding walls, openings, and terrain match best. Copies continue from already-written neighbours, so the artist's strokes, clusters, and small openings carry over whole. The near exemplar's context is the artist's near wall tidied by the same rules as generated openings, so synthesis also restores the artist's ragged edges. Detailing reaches up to twelve tiles into middle and far walls, eight into near walls, and two into an opening. Manual near-background markers add coverage to the generated near wall before detailing; use them for fixups rather than to shape the plane. Ice and tundra share the near openings and differ in their exemplars. Middle/far pairs blend both biomes' openings and artwork by depth in camera space, accounting for each plane's parallax so the background follows the world transition.

79.body:
tools/backgrounds/generate.py builds three paired variants per map from its footprint, independent of the randomly selected terrain templates. Exemplars and middle/far LDtk definitions live under tools/backgrounds/source. Every cave layer leaves the player-spawn chunk empty for the surface backdrop. Shared tilesheets stay under assets/levels/tiles/ldtk_rules; the runtime LDtk project owns terrain, near background, and object definitions. Depth-mode pairs combine both authored tilesheets in one native-size atlas before baking, so runtime loading keeps the ordinary bank path. Use Python 3.11+ and the pinned requirements: python3 -m venv tools/backgrounds/.venv
tools/backgrounds/.venv/bin/pip install -r tools/backgrounds/requirements.txt
tools/backgrounds/.venv/bin/python tools/backgrounds/generate.py
tools/backgrounds/.venv/bin/python tools/backgrounds/generate.py --level assets/levels/level_test.png
tools/backgrounds/.venv/bin/python tools/backgrounds/generate.py --biome tundra --preview /absolute/dir --preview-only
tools/backgrounds/.venv/bin/python tools/backgrounds/exemplars.py path/to/level.01.ldtk The default command processes all map PNGs with --biome depth; custom levels use ice by default. --preview DIR also writes each pair's unblurred far and middle planes composited over the sky; --preview-only skips the banks. --biome ice or --biome tundra generates a single-biome inspection set; tundra banks go under background_bank/tundra/, which the runtime does not load. --map assets/levels/maps/map1.png restricts the input and --variant 2 rebuilds one pair. Explicit input paths are relative to the working directory; other paths resolve from the script. Custom PNGs need a bank under custom/<filename stem>; custom stems must be unique within a shipped asset set. Output lives under assets/levels/background_bank/<map>/<variant>-<layer>/. Variants are 0–2; layer 1 is middle and layer 2 is far. Each directory contains a manifest, numbered blurred RGBA chunks, and corresponding -coverage.png masks. The manifest records format version, dimensions, map/source hashes, and chunk bounds. Two tiles of outer padding, blur radii of three/five pixels, and one-pixel filtering gutters preserve the layer appearance. Three pairs mean six logical layers per map, split into bounded files. Regenerate after changing a map footprint, exemplar, shared tilesheet, or generator. Density and spacing constants sit at the top of openings.py; raising FILL opens more of each plane and lets more light through. Runtime loading checks map hashes and geometry and reports invalid or missing banks explicitly; there is no procedural fallback. The Python validation suite also checks source freshness and shared gutters. The request seed selects a pair; SEEKER_BACKGROUND_VARIANT=0, 1, or 2 overrides selection for inspection.

8.body: On a lonely expedition, a Seeker feels a pull unlike anything before and follows it to an icy planet whose richness seems almost too perfect. The surface is frozen and exposed. Life shelters in caves beneath the ice, warmed by the planet's heat. The deeper you go, the warmer it gets and the stranger, more beautiful, and more dangerous the ecosystems become. Others have come here too, scientists, opportunists, caretakers, and worshippers among them, each with their own idea of what the planet is for. Something near the planet's core seems to be calling. What it is, and why it calls, is the heart of the story. Ancient alien demigods called Guardians watch over the planet. Their origins are a mystery.

80.body: The player-spawn template is an open crater under the sky. surface_backdrop.rs draws the sky, high clouds, distant range, nearer hills, and the crater's far wall as one-chunk-wide images from assets/levels/surface, placed by spawn-chunk rows. Their parallax is measured from the player spawn, so the resting capsule view shows the artwork as authored; below that view the layers stay fixed to the world so they never sink into the caves. The opaque sky sits in front of the middle and far cave planes, and the far wall in front of the near plane, because those planes' parallax shifts other cave content under the spawn chunk. The same module publishes an OpenSkyRegion in which foreground fog clears above the crater rim. Fullscreen depth darkness is measured from the surface above the capsule: it stays at zero through the first chunk below and eases in over the next. A spawn template may have an intact-ground sibling with the same file name under assets/levels/chunks/pre_impact/; only its #000000 terrain pixels are read. impact_crater.rs bakes that terrain, plus the cave directly below any opening it closes (bounded, deeper than any pre-impact view), as hidden ImpactIntact surface patches beside the ImpactFormed crater patches. Collision always uses the formed crater. The landing cinematic in game/src/game/intro.rs shows the intact ground until the impact. tools/surface_art/generate.py generates the backdrop layers and the cinematic's effect sheets under assets/animations/intro (Pillow and NumPy; the background requirements suffice). Its colors come from the ice-biome tilesets so the surface continues into the caves. Keep its layer rows in sync with surface_backdrop.rs; --preview /absolute/dir writes composited views at several camera heights and effect strips.
